## Observations

1. The first operation colors the entire grid, and each subsequent nonempty square lies inside the previous one.
2. A square from operation \(k\) contains cell \((r,c)\) exactly when \(k \le r,c \le N+1-k\). Thus the last operation to color the cell has index \(\min(r,c,N+1-r,N+1-c)\).
3. The final character is `#` if the last operation index is odd and `.` if it is even.
4. The output contains \(N^2\) characters across \(N\) rows, and each cell's character can be determined independently.

## Solution sketch

> A square from operation \(k\) contains cell \((r,c)\) exactly when \(k \le r,c \le N+1-k\). Thus the last operation to color the cell has index \(\min(r,c,N+1-r,N+1-c)\).

1. Read \(N\), then visit the cells in row order using 1-based indices. For each cell, compute the minimum of the four terms above. This directly identifies the operation whose color survives, so there is no need to simulate overwrites.

> The final character is `#` if the last operation index is odd and `.` if it is even.

2. Append the character determined by the index's parity to the current row. No special cases are needed: for \(N=1\), the only cell has index 1; for even \(N\), all four central cells have index \(N/2\) and therefore receive the same color.

> The output contains \(N^2\) characters across \(N\) rows, and each cell's character can be determined independently.

3. Print each row as soon as it is complete, then discard it. The algorithm takes \(\Theta(N^2)\) time, which is optimal for writing the output, and uses \(O(N)\) auxiliary space to hold one row.
